title: No-Code Statistical Inference: Understanding Data, Uncertainty, and Evidence

dataset_source.name: Rdatasets public CSV archive
dataset_source.access: Public files are vendored locally for this app. No API key or runtime network connection is required.

data_pathways.demonstration: One public dataset selected and demonstrated by the instructor in every module.

data_pathways.participant_upload: Participants may upload their own CSV dataset in every module and use the module workflow after selecting compatible variables.

days.title: Day 1 — Data, variation, and uncertainty
days.general_theme: Foundations of data, variation, and uncertainty
days.introduction: Day 1 establishes the language of data, estimands, variation, sampling distributions, and uncertainty. After a ten-minute orientation, ten 17-minute modules each begin with a rigorous presentation and then move to a public-data demonstration and a distinct BYOD activity.

modules.title: Observational units, variables, populations, and samples
modules.presentation_focus: Define observational units, variables, populations, samples, parameters, statistics, and the distinction between a scientific target and an observed dataset.
modules.notation: Let X_1, …, X_n denote observed values sampled from a population distribution F; a parameter θ is a feature of F, while a statistic T(X_1, …, X_n) is a function of the sample.
results: A statistic and a parameter are conceptually different objects.
The population of inference must be specified before a sample can support a general claim.

demonstration.name: Iris
demonstration.activity: Identify observational units and variable types, then distinguish species-specific sample summaries from population targets.

modules.title: Measurement scales, coding, and data quality
modules.presentation_focus: Introduce nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio scales; distinguish recorded codes from substantive constructs; and identify missingness and data-quality concerns.
modules.notation: A variable X can be numeric without being interval-scaled; transformations and arithmetic summaries require assumptions about the scale and coding of X.
results: Variable coding determines which comparisons and summaries are meaningful.
Missing values are part of the data-generating and measurement process, not merely a software inconvenience.

demonstration.name: New York Air Quality
demonstration.activity: Audit variable types, identify missing ozone and solar-radiation values, and specify an analysis-ready subset.

modules.title: Distributional summaries: centre, spread, and shape
modules.presentation_focus: Define the mean, median, variance, standard deviation, interquartile range, quantiles, skewness, and the role of robust summaries.
modules.notation: For values x_1, …, x_n, x̄ = n⁻¹Σ_i x_i and s² = (n−1)⁻¹Σ_i(x_i−x̄)²; the median minimizes the sum of absolute deviations.
results: The mean and standard deviation are sensitive to extreme observations.
Quantiles and robust summaries can communicate distributional structure that one average obscures.

demonstration.activity: Compare mean/standard deviation with median/interquartile range for height and weight, then interpret their different purposes.

modules.title: Visual evidence and exploratory data analysis
modules.presentation_focus: State the purpose and limitations of histograms, boxplots, scatterplots, conditional summaries, and visual detection of unusual observations.
modules.notation: The empirical distribution function is F̂_n(x) = n⁻¹Σ_i I(X_i ≤ x); graphical displays approximate features of F̂_n or of conditional distributions.
results: A graphic is an estimator or display of data structure, not a proof of a model.
Patterns should be checked against variable definitions, sampling mechanisms, and potential measurement artifacts.

modules.title: Random variation and repeated sampling
modules.presentation_focus: Introduce randomness, sampling variability, repeated-sampling thought experiments, and the distinction between a realised sample and its sampling distribution.
modules.notation: If X_1, …, X_n are iid with mean μ and variance σ², then E[X̄] = μ and Var(X̄) = σ²/n.
results: The observed sample mean is one realisation of a random estimator.
Larger samples reduce the variance of the sample mean when the iid model is appropriate.

demonstration.name: Old Faithful Eruptions
demonstration.activity: Use repeated subsamples to see how estimates of waiting time vary across equally sized samples.

modules.title: Sampling distributions and the central limit theorem
modules.presentation_focus: Define a sampling distribution, standard error, normal approximation, and the regularity conditions behind the central limit theorem.
modules.notation: Under iid sampling with finite variance, √n(X̄−μ)/σ converges in distribution to N(0,1) as n grows.
results: The central limit theorem concerns an estimator over repeated samples, not the raw-data shape alone.
Normal approximations require context-specific checks rather than mechanical invocation.

demonstration.activity: Simulate repeated samples of tree volume and compare the raw distribution with the distribution of sample means.

modules.title: Standard errors and confidence intervals
modules.presentation_focus: Define standard error, confidence procedures, interval width, confidence level, and long-run coverage.
modules.notation: An approximate 1−α interval for μ is X̄ ± z_(1−α/2) SE(X̄); the procedure targets P_μ{μ ∈ C(X)} = 1−α under stated assumptions.
results: A confidence interval is not a probability distribution over a fixed parameter in the frequentist interpretation.
Interval width depends on variability, sample size, and chosen confidence level.

demonstration.activity: Estimate mean stopping distance and compare confidence intervals under different sample sizes and confidence levels.

modules.title: Bootstrap confidence intervals
modules.presentation_focus: Define the empirical distribution, resampling with replacement, bootstrap replicates, bootstrap standard error, and percentile intervals.
modules.notation: The empirical distribution F̂_n places mass 1/n on each observation; θ̂* is the statistic recomputed on a sample drawn from F̂_n.
results: Bootstrap methods approximate sampling variation through the empirical distribution.
Resampling cannot repair selection bias, an ill-defined estimand, or data that do not represent the target population.

modules.title: Monte Carlo simulation and numerical uncertainty
modules.presentation_focus: Introduce simulation design, pseudo-random draws, Monte Carlo estimators, reproducible seeds, and simulation error.
modules.notation: For independent simulation outputs Z_1, …, Z_B, the Monte Carlo estimator B⁻¹Σ_b Z_b has standard error proportional to B^(−1/2).
results: A simulation estimate has its own numerical uncertainty.
Seeds support reproducibility but do not validate the underlying statistical model.

modules.title: Assumptions, outliers, and analytical readiness
modules.presentation_focus: Define an assumption, an outlier, leverage, influence, transformations, and the difference between data screening and post-hoc result selection.

days.title: Day 2 — Tests, comparisons, and categorical inference
days.general_theme: Evidence from comparisons, tests, and categorical data
days.introduction: Day 2 develops formal comparisons and categorical-data reasoning. Every module states its estimand, assumptions, and reference distribution before participants see a demonstrated analysis and work with a separate public BYOD dataset or an upload.

modules.title: Estimands, hypotheses, and null reference distributions
modules.presentation_focus: Define null and alternative hypotheses, test statistics, null distributions, significance level, p-values, and the relation between tests and estimands.
modules.notation: For H_0: θ=θ_0 and test statistic T, the p-value is P_{H_0}(|T|≥|t_obs|) for a two-sided reference rule.
results: A p-value is conditional on the null model and the specified test statistic.
A non-significant result is not evidence that an effect is exactly zero.

demonstration.name: Tooth Growth
demonstration.activity: Frame a supplement comparison as an estimand and test it at a selected dose, before interpreting the p-value.

modules.title: Effect sizes and practical significance
modules.presentation_focus: Define raw differences, standardized mean differences, uncertainty intervals, practical thresholds, and the difference between statistical and substantive significance.
modules.notation: For two groups, Cohen's d = (X̄_2−X̄_1)/s_p, where s_p is a pooled within-group standard deviation under its stated convention.
results: Effect sizes require scale and context for interpretation.
An effect can be precisely estimated yet substantively negligible, or important yet imprecisely estimated.

modules.title: Independent two-group comparisons
modules.presentation_focus: Present the independent-samples mean difference, Welch's t procedure, standard-error construction, confidence intervals, and assumptions about group formation.
modules.notation: T = (X̄_1−X̄_2)/√(s_1²/n_1+s_2²/n_2), with a Welch–Satterthwaite reference degrees-of-freedom approximation.
results: Welch's procedure does not assume equal population variances.
Causal language requires an appropriate design, not only a two-group test.

modules.title: Paired and repeated-measures comparisons
modules.presentation_focus: Define paired differences, within-unit dependence, repeated observations, longitudinal structure, and why an independent-sample analysis can be inappropriate for paired data.
modules.notation: For paired values (X_i,Y_i), analyse D_i=Y_i−X_i; the paired t statistic is T=D̄/(s_D/√n).
results: Pairing can reduce variance when within-unit correlation is used correctly.
Repeated measurements require clarity about the observational unit and the dependence structure.

modules.title: Analysis of variance and multi-group questions
modules.presentation_focus: Introduce between-group and within-group variation, the one-way ANOVA model, F statistics, omnibus tests, contrasts, and multiplicity-aware follow-up questions.
modules.notation: In Y_ij=μ+α_j+ε_ij, the F statistic compares mean-square variation between groups with mean-square variation within groups.
results: An omnibus ANOVA test does not identify which group differences are present.
Planned contrasts and post-hoc comparisons should be distinguished and documented.

modules.title: Nonparametric and permutation approaches
modules.presentation_focus: Introduce rank-based tests, randomization/permutation logic, exchangeability, and when a distribution-free label is misleading.
modules.notation: Under exchangeability under H_0, a permutation distribution is formed by recomputing T over relabelings consistent with the null hypothesis.
results: Permutation validity depends on an exchangeability condition tied to the design.
Rank-based procedures answer questions about distributions or stochastic ordering that need not equal a mean comparison.

modules.title: Categorical variables and conditional probabilities
modules.presentation_focus: Define joint, marginal, and conditional distributions; risk differences; relative risks; odds; and the role of stratification.
modules.notation: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B); a risk difference is P(Y=1|X=1)−P(Y=1|X=0) when these probabilities are well defined.
results: Conditional probabilities must identify the conditioning event clearly.
Association in observational data does not by itself identify a causal effect.

modules.title: Contingency tables and chi-square inference
modules.presentation_focus: Define expected counts, Pearson's chi-square statistic, independence models, reference degrees of freedom, and sparse-table cautions.
modules.notation: E_ij=(row total_i×column total_j)/N and X²=Σ_ij(O_ij−E_ij)²/E_ij.
results: The chi-square approximation requires independent observational units and adequate expected counts.
An aggregate table may require frequency weights rather than row counts.

modules.title: Stratification, confounding, and Simpson-type reversals
modules.presentation_focus: Define a confounder, stratified comparison, marginal association, conditional association, and why aggregation can alter apparent relationships.
modules.notation: A marginal association P(Y|X) can differ from a stratum-specific association P(Y|X,Z) when the distribution of Z differs across X.
results: Stratification is a design and modeling decision, not a universal cure for confounding.
A reversal across aggregation levels should trigger examination of mechanisms, design, and variable definitions.

days.title: Day 3 — Regression, prediction, diagnostics, and reproducibility
days.general_theme: Conditional modelling, prediction, diagnostics, and reproducibility
days.introduction: Day 3 treats regression and prediction as transparent conditional models. Each module separates a public demonstration from a distinct BYOD data choice and gives participants an upload path for their own tabular data.

modules.title: Simple linear regression and conditional means
modules.presentation_focus: Introduce the conditional mean function, simple linear model, least squares, fitted values, residuals, slope, intercept, and the conditional interpretation of a coefficient.
modules.notation: In Y=β_0+β_1X+ε, ordinary least squares selects β̂ to minimize Σ_i(Y_i−β_0−β_1X_i)².
results: A slope estimates a conditional linear association under the model specification.
A regression line does not establish causation without design and substantive assumptions.

demonstration.name: Automobile Data
demonstration.activity: Model miles per gallon as a function of weight, interpret the fitted slope, and inspect the residual definition.

modules.title: Multiple regression and adjustment
modules.presentation_focus: Define multiple linear regression, partial regression coefficients, covariate adjustment, reference coding, omitted variables, and conditional versus marginal effects.
modules.notation: In Y=β_0+β_1X_1+…+β_pX_p+ε, β_j is the model-based change in E[Y|X] per unit X_j holding other included X variables fixed.
results: Adjustment changes the estimand and requires a substantive rationale for included variables.
Holding variables fixed in a model is not equivalent to experimental control.

demonstration.activity: Fit a sales model using price and advertising, then compare the conditional interpretation with a marginal scatterplot.

modules.title: Regression uncertainty and coefficient intervals
modules.presentation_focus: Introduce coefficient standard errors, confidence intervals, tests, model degrees of freedom, and the distinction between coefficient uncertainty and predictive uncertainty.
modules.notation: An approximate coefficient interval is β̂_j ± t_(1−α/2,df)SE(β̂_j) under the fitted-model assumptions.
results: A coefficient interval is conditional on the model, the observed covariates, and the sampling/design assumptions.
Statistical significance should not be used as a substitute for model comparison or substantive interpretation.

demonstration.activity: Estimate a simple credit-balance relationship and interpret a coefficient interval together with the scale of the variables.

modules.title: Nonlinearity, transformations, and model specification
modules.presentation_focus: Define functional form, transformations, polynomial terms, interaction terms, residual patterns, and the risks of specification search.
modules.notation: A transformed model replaces X or Y with g(X) or h(Y); a polynomial specification augments E[Y|X] with powers such as X².
results: A transformation changes the scale and interpretation of model parameters.
Improved in-sample fit alone does not justify a more complex specification.

demonstration.name: House Prices
demonstration.activity: Compare raw and transformed price relationships, then explain how the interpretation changes with the chosen scale.

modules.title: Logistic regression, odds, and predicted probabilities
modules.presentation_focus: Introduce binary outcomes, probability models, log-odds, logistic links, odds ratios, and the difference between odds and probability.
modules.notation: logit[P(Y=1|X=x)] = log(p(x)/(1−p(x))) = β_0+x^Tβ; exp(β_j) is a conditional odds ratio.
results: An odds ratio is not generally a risk ratio.
Predicted probabilities depend on the covariate pattern and the model specification.

modules.title: Binary-outcome prediction and classification thresholds

modules.notation: A threshold rule predicts Ŷ=I[p̂(X)≥c]; changing c changes the confusion matrix and its error trade-offs.
results: A classification threshold encodes a decision and its consequences.
Accuracy alone can be misleading with imbalanced outcomes or unequal error costs.

modules.title: Calibration, discrimination, and probability communication
modules.presentation_focus: Define calibration, discrimination, predicted risk, calibration plots, and how probability estimates should be communicated to nontechnical audiences.
modules.notation: A calibrated model satisfies approximately P(Y=1|p̂(X)=p)≈p over relevant groups; discrimination concerns separation of outcome classes by scores.
results: Good discrimination does not guarantee calibrated probabilities.
Probability statements should identify the model, population, horizon, and uncertainty.

modules.title: Diagnostics, influence, and sensitivity analysis
modules.presentation_focus: Define residual diagnostics, leverage, influence, influential cases, alternative specifications, and transparent analytical sensitivity analysis.
modules.notation: The residual is e_i=y_i−ŷ_i; sensitivity analysis compares estimates over a pre-specified or transparently reported set of defensible choices.
results: A model can fit a summary well while failing diagnostically important patterns.
Sensitivity analysis reveals dependence on choices; it does not eliminate substantive uncertainty.

modules.presentation_focus: Define training data, test data, resampling, generalization, prediction error, data leakage, and the distinction between model fitting and model evaluation.
modules.notation: For held-out outcomes y_i and predictions ŷ_i, MSPE=m⁻¹Σ_i(y_i−ŷ_i)²; evaluation is valid only when the test relationship matches the target use case.
results: In-sample fit and out-of-sample performance answer different questions.
A test set must be protected from model-selection decisions to serve as a final evaluation set.

modules.title: Reproducible no-code workflows and transparent reporting
modules.presentation_focus: Define computational reproducibility, data provenance, analysis specifications, software environments, seeds, versioned data, output records, and limits of app-generated reports.
modules.notation: A reproducible result is conditional on a documented dataset D, transformation A, model M, settings S, software environment E, and random seed r where relevant.
results: No-code applications should make assumptions and provenance visible rather than conceal them.
Reproducibility is necessary but not sufficient for validity or causal interpretation.
